newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian-Gold - Price drop seen lifting demand.
newsitem.headline: Asian-Gold - Price drop seen lifting demand.

text.p: The slide in spot gold prices to around $352 an ounce on Friday, from about $358 at the start of the week, on renewed fears of central bank sales should once again lift physical demand in Asia, dealers said.
But there were signs that the price fall was now bottoming out and a sharp rebound would quickly squeeze emerging demand, they added.
By 0630 GMT spot gold was trading at $352.45/75 an ounce in Hong Kong, down from the opening at $352.70/353.20.
Traders saw support at $352 an ounce and said prices were more likely to go up than down.
"Customers are still short at the moment," one dealer said.
"If the market can't break the downside, then gold can go as high as $360," said one dealer when asked for his outlook for next week.
"Sentiment is mixed, with new fears of the Swiss Bank selling gold and that could dampen sentiment."
News this week that Switzerland's central bank is proposing to sell gold to fund an aid foundation for victims of the Holocaust has overshadowed the market this week, dealers said.
"If prices are headed lower, we should see demand picking up again. When gold was at US$360 (an ounce), the buying just died," a dealer for a U.S. financial house in Singapore said.
The demand picture was rekindled after gold prices in New York fell $6.0 an ounce during Wednesday's trading session.
"I think that if the price falls to around $350, demand will definitely get better," the dealer said.
Another dealer for a Singapore-based bank forecast that demand in the coming days "will be quite strong. If gold slides to $345, you'll see demand accelerating."
The dealer said brisk orders will probably come in from traditional buyers in Hong Kong, China, India and Indonesia if the price of the yellow metal becomes more attractive.

Singapore premiums were steady to slightly firmer at 120-140 U.S. cents over spot London prices from last week's 110-140 cents and traders in the city-state predict they may rise into next week if demand picks up as expected.
"We're slightly off the peaks in the premiums compared to the ones we saw last month. But premiums will climb back to those levels if buying picks up," one bank dealer said.

Singapore premiums climbed to as high as 160 U.S. cents over spot London prices in February and even reached 170 cents in Hong Kong as physical buying strengthened when gold was languishing near the $340 an ounce level.
